questions.question: Explain the difference between a wage and a salary in terms of the UNIT of payment, and how that difference decides which journal each will use.
questions.expected_answer: A wage is calculated from time worked — so much per hour — and paid weekly or fortnightly, so its unit is the hour; a salary is a fixed annual amount for a position, paid in twelve equal monthly instalments, so its unit is the year. Wage earners are recorded in the Wages Journal, salary earners in the Salaries Journal. The wage responds to the hours of the week; the salary stays stable with growth arriving annually through the notch.

questions.question: Read the scale R96 000 × R9 600 — R144 000: name its three parts, give the monthly pay in year two of service, and calculate how many increments it takes to reach the top.
questions.expected_answer: Starting notch R96 000 per year; annual increment (notch increase) R9 600; ceiling R144 000. After one completed year the employee stands on R105 600 per year, which is R8 800 per month. The distance from bottom to top is R48 000; divided by the notch of R9 600 that is five increments, so the ceiling is reached at the start of year six.

questions.question: Run S. Dlamini's week to gross (R40 per hour, 45 normal hours, 4 hours evening overtime), showing the labelled lines the marking rewards, and state what changes if the overtime falls on a public holiday.
questions.expected_answer: Normal pay: 45 × R40 = R1 800. Overtime rate: time and a half = R60 per hour, written as its own line. Overtime pay: 4 × R60 = R240. Gross: R2 040. On a public holiday the multiplier becomes double time, so the rate line changes to R80 and the overtime line to R320, giving gross R2 120 — the same skeleton with one substituted rate, and the rate must always be derived as its own step before multiplying by hours.
